description: Hi, I'm Shayan, a 4th-year CS student in Toronto with front-end and back-end experience and an interest in UI and AI. I'm building a team to create software that monitors astronaut health. Join for real-world impact and hands-on experience, whether it's your first hackathon or not. Looking for data science/ML, UI/UX, back-end, or health science skills. Curious and excited to build? Message me!
summary:
As humanity prepares for missions to the Moon, Mars, and beyond, astronauts face a critical challenge: maintaining their health when medical assistance from Earth may be millions of kilometres and significant communication delays away.

Space6ix is an interactive, 3D astronaut health-monitoring and onboard decision-support platform designed to make healthcare more accessible, understandable, and autonomous during long-duration space missions.

Our solution integrates physiological indicators, including cardiovascular measurements, oxygen saturation, blood biomarkers, sleep, and other health observations, into an interactive anatomical model. By visually connecting health data to relevant body systems, Space6ix helps astronauts recognize concerning changes, explore potential contributing factors, and access information to support timely decisions.

Drawing on NASA's Open Science Data Repository, published spaceflight research, and simulated mission scenarios, our prototype demonstrates how scientific evidence and intuitive technology can support future crew healthcare.

Our vision extends beyond monitoring: we aim to empower astronauts to understand their health and respond confidently when Earth cannot answer immediately.

Because the future of space exploration is not just about how far humanity can travel, but how safely we can bring humanity along.
details:
What does it do, and how does it work?

SOMA (Spaceflight Organ Monitoring Application), helps astronauts review health measurements, track changes over time, and record check-ins. An interactive 3D body lets crew members select a health signal and view its measurements, trends, and context. The app shows how Earth-standard and space-adapted rules interpret the same readings and explains why a signal was flagged.

What are the benefits and intended impact?

SOMA gives crews a way to notice changes, document concerns, and share a clearer record with a flight surgeon. In the simulated 90-minute communications outage, the crew logs observations at checkpoints, identifies missing information, and queues a handoff. Once contact returns, the flight surgeon can review the timeline and send a follow-up through Earth link. The intended impact is better continuity of support when crews have limited access to Earth.

What tools did we use?

We built the interface with React, TypeScript, and Three.js, the backend with Node.js and SQLite, and the research data pipeline with Python, pandas, and scikit-learn. We used NASA research datasets for blood counts, metabolic and immune measurements, mouse bone research, and environmental radiation telemetry. The demo uses simulated crew readings.

What makes it creative, and what did we consider?

The 3D view connects a health signal using bodily sensors in the spacesuit and to the ISS, to a workflow the crew can practice. A crew member can review a reading, log a concern, and prepare a handoff for Earth in the same app. We considered altered gravity, radiation, disrupted sleep, isolation, missing readings, crew privacy, and communication delays. The drill runs locally without cloud AI, and the app supports monitoring and training while leaving diagnosis to medical professionals.
